source_text: Icrrur secundum magnitudinem non est cognoscere Deum ; impossibile est enim mensurari Patrem ; secundum autem dilectionem ejus, hee est enim que nos per Verbum ejus perducit ad Deum, obedientes ei semper discimus quoniam est tantus Deus, et ipse est qui per semetipsum constituit, et elegit, et adornavit, qui est secundum nos. Et nos igitur cum his que continentur ab eo, factisumus. Et hic est de quo Scriptura ait; Ht plasmavit Deus hominem, limum terre accipiens, et insufflavit in faciem ejus Jjlatum vite. Non ergo angeli fecerunt, nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis preter Verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre uniNec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quie ipse apud se preefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit, ad quos et loquitur, dicens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; ipse a semetipso substantiam creaturarum, et exemplum factorum, et figuram in mundo ornamentorum accipiens.
pass_a_gloss: It is not to know God according to magnitude; for it is impossible to measure the Father; but according to his love, this is what leads us to God through his Word, obeying him we always learn that God is so great, and he is the one who establishes and chooses and adorns through himself, who is according to us. And we therefore have been made with those things which are contained by him. And this is what Scripture says: That God formed man, taking clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life. Therefore, angels did not make us, nor did they form us, nor could angels make the image of God, nor anyone else except the Word of the Lord, nor a power far removed from the Father. For God did not need these things to do what he had predetermined to do, as if he did not have his own hands. For the Word and Wisdom, the Son and Spirit, are always present to him, through whom and in whom he freely and willingly made all things, and to whom he speaks, saying: Let us make man in our image and likeness; he himself taking the substance of creatures and the model of things made and the figure of ornaments in the world from himself.

bible_refs.note: God formed man, taking clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life

pass_b_english: We cannot know God by measuring his magnitude, because the Father cannot be measured; but his love draws us to him through his Word, and as we obey that Word we keep learning just how great God truly is. He himself, in his own person, establishes, chooses, and adorns all things in a way that relates to us, and we ourselves have been made from what he contains. This is what Scripture declares: "Then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Angels did not make us, nor did they shape us; angels could not fashion the image of God, nor could anyone else except the Word of the Lord, and certainly no power that stands far removed from the Father. God did not need such beings to carry out what he had predetermined, as if he lacked his own hands. The Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present to him; through them and in them he freely and willingly made all things. He speaks to them, saying, "Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness" (Genesis 1:26), himself drawing the substance of creatures, the pattern of his works, and the form of the world's adornments from his own being.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that correctly identifies the Scripture citations (Genesis 2:7 and Genesis 1:26) alluded to in the Latin (Ht plasmavit Deus hominem... and Faciamus hominem...). The distinction between 'through himself' (per semetipsum) and 'from himself' (a semetipso) is maintained.
